rationale: A wins because it keeps its sharper angles closer to the supplied record. “Mercury Is Offering Consumer Accounts Without a Bank Charter” turns a real fact into a real consumer-protection story; B’s “What the SVB windfall became: 200,000 businesses, a profit claim, and now a consumer bank” smuggles in causation and calls Mercury a bank while the brief explicitly says it lacks a charter. B is useful, but it keeps stepping over the evidence line, and reporters notice that before they notice your clever frame.
gaps_in_A: “Mercury's name recognition was built entirely on being the startup-banking alternative” overstates the brief. The facts say Mercury became well known after SVB, not that SVB built its entire name recognition.
“Mercury's playbook runs opposite to the consumer-to-business neobank trajectory most competitors have tried” imports a market-history claim the update did not supply.

“Mercury Has 200,000 Business Customers. It Just Started Pitching Them Personally.” is a useful frame, but the headline implies Mercury is targeting existing business customers personally before the facts prove that.
A misses a clean direct-competition angle against neobanks and incumbents as its own lens; it gestures at the market in the category angle but does not fully exploit the conflict.
gaps_in_B: “What the SVB windfall became” is the worst overreach. The update does not say the 200,000 businesses or profitability came from SVB fallout.
“the bank startups fled to after SVB” is too loose twice: Mercury is not a bank charter, and “fled to” is stronger than the supplied “became well known as an alternative.”
“now a consumer bank” contradicts the partner-bank/no-charter fact. That is not color; that is a reporter correction waiting to happen.
“founders and employees who already bank at those 200,000 companies” invents the employee relationship. The fact is 200,000 businesses, not their employees as reachable personal-banking prospects.
